title: Conditional Expected Casualty Exception for Failures Resulting in an Uncontrolled Atmospheric Return
content: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION Federal Aviation Administration 14 CFR Parts 401 and 450 [Docket No.: FAA-2026-9942; Notice No. 26-20] RIN 2120-AM33 Conditional Expected Casualty Exception for Failures Resulting in an Uncontrolled Atmospheric Return AGENCY: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT). ACTION: Notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM). SUMMARY: FAA proposes to amend its commercial space launch and reentry licensing regulations to streamline the licensing process and reduce regulatory burden for license applicants. Specifically, FAA proposes to allow a launch and reentry vehicle operator to protect against high consequence events during an uncontrolled atmospheric return by showing that there would be sufficient breakup of the vehicle to ensure protection against a single event expected to produce multiple casualties. ADDRESSES: Send comments identified by docket number FAA-2026-9942 using any of the following methods: • Federal eRulemaking Portal: Go to www.regulations.gov and follow the online instructions for sending your comments electronically. • Mail: Send comments to Docket Operations; U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT), 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, West Building, 5th Floor (W58-213), Washington, DC 20590-0001. • Hand Delivery or Courier: Take comments to Docket Operations in Room W58-213 of the West Building, 5th Floor at 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590 between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays. • Fax: Fax comments to Docket Operations at (202) 493-2251. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: I. Overview In accordance with Executive Order (E.O.) 14335 “Enabling Competition in the Commercial Space Industry,” FAA proposes to amend its commercial space launch and reentry regulations at 14 CFR part 450 to further streamline the commercial licensing process. Specifically, FAA proposes to add an option by which applicants may comply with the high consequence event protection requirements in § 450.101(c). The proposed rule would allow an applicant to meet the requirement for an uncontrolled atmospheric return (UAR), commonly called a “random reentry,” by showing that the UAR would result in sufficient breakup of the vehicle, including all vehicle components and undeployed payloads, to ensure protection against a single event expected to produce multiple casualties. II. Authority for This Rulemaking The Commercial Space Launch Act of 1984, as amended and codified at 51 U.S.C. 50901-50924, authorizes the Secretary of Transportation to oversee, license, and regulate commercial launch and reentry activities, and the operation of launch and reentry sites within the United States (U.S.) or as carried out by U.S. citizens. Section 50905 directs the Secretary to exercise this responsibility consistent with public health and safety, safety of property, and the national security and foreign policy interests of the United States. In addition, section 50903 requires the Secretary to encourage, facilitate, and promote commercial space launches and reentries by the private sector. As codified in 49 CFR 1.83(b), the Secretary has delegated authority to the FAA Administrator to carry out these functions. III. Background FAAhasestablishedcommercial space regulations governing licensing of launch and reentry in 14 CFR chapter III. On December 10, 2020, FAA issued a final ruleconsolidatingall substantive launch and reentry licensing regulations into a new part 450 (85 FR 79566) that went into effect on March 10, 2021. On August 13, 2025,the President issued E.O. 14335, “Enabling Competition in the Commercial Space Industry,” requiring the Secretary of Transportation to “reevaluate, amend, or rescind” the part 450 regulations for the purpose of further streamlining the commercial licensing process. This proposed rule is being published in furtherance of this executive order. In accordance with current FAA guidance, high consequence events include incidents that could involve multiple casualties, massive toxic exposures, extensive property or environmental damage, or events that jeopardize the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States. 1 The term “high consequence events” does not generally include incidents that result in only one casualty. The potential for any casualties remains covered by the individual and collective risk criteria in § 450.101(a) and (b). The objective of high consequence protection is to provide additional constraints beyond the individual and collective risk criteria. 1 See Advisory Circular 450.101-1B, “High Consequence Event Protection,” dated May 03, 2024, available at: www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_450.101-1B.pdf; see also Footnote 65 in final rule titled “Streamlined Launch and Reentry Requirements” (85 FR 79566). Currently, in accordance with § 450.101(c), an operator must protect against a high consequence event by one of three methods: flight abort, ensuring that conditional expected casualties (CE C ) would fall below a specified threshold, or demonstrated reliability. However, these three methods are not well-attuned for protection against high consequence events during a UAR. A UAR, commonly called a “random reentry,” occurs when a vehicle makes an uncontrolled descent from orbit as a result of natural orbital decay, rather than as a result of action by the operator. Currently, no UARs are close to attaining the demonstrated reliability necessary to protect against high consequence events, which makes compliance with § 450.101(c)(3) improbable at this time. Likewise, any vehicle flight that could be aborted in accordance with § 450.101(c)(1) is not a UAR because the operator is able to accomplish a controlled end to the flight; a UAR is always an uncontrolled end to flight. Thus, operators currently must comply with the CE C requirement in § 450.101(c)(2), which can be a labor-intensive calculation. IV. Discussion of the Proposal The proposed rule would amend § 450.101(c)(2) to allow an operator to demonstrate protection against a high consequence event resulting from a UAR by showing that the UAR would result in sufficient breakup of the vehicle, including all vehicle components and payloads, to ensure protection against a single event expected to produce multiple casualties. The proposed method of demonstrating compliance to high consequence events for UARs provides an equivalent level of safety to the current requirements. An uncontrolled atmospheric return is fundamentally a return in which the operator has no control over the eventual impact site of the vehicle. Accordingly, the proposal would define “uncontrolled atmospheric return” in § 401.7 to include two characteristics that limit the definition to cover only those returns over which the operator exercises no control. The first proposed defining characteristic of a UAR would be that only natural forces cause the orbit of an object to decay and eventually impact the Earth or burn up in the atmosphere. Natural forces that cause orbital decay include aerodynamic drag, gravitational variations, solar radiation, and third-body gravitational effects. A perigee of 70 nautical miles (nm) or greater is considered the threshold of being in orbit (see definition of “Deorbit” in § 401.7). Thus, a scenario in which propulsion (which is not a natural force) reduces the perigee below the 70 nm threshold would not be considered a UAR. However, a propulsion system that fails before the perigee reaches the threshold could result in a UAR. The second proposed defining characteristic of a UAR would be that the operator lacks control over the trajectory. Thus, a flight that uses orientation to control aerodynamic forces to reduce the perigee below the 70 nm threshold would not be considered a UAR. Likewise, a vehicle that falls out of orbit due to natural forces, but which an operator may abort or otherwise guide, would not be considered a UAR. The proposed method of demonstrating compliance to high consequence events at proposed § 450.101(c)(2)(ii) would only be available for UARs (as opposed to controlled returns) because UARs have unique properties. First, the impact probability distributions from a UAR, which are the subject of § 450.123(b), are extremely large. It is most likely that debris would impact in areas with relatively low population density because high-density populations are concentrated in small areas. In addition, when multiple fragments survive deorbit during a UAR, they are generally dispersed over a large geographical area, so it is unlikely that separate fragments would injure multiple people from the same UAR as long as the collective risk safety criterion in § 450.101(a) or (b) is satisfied. The proposed requirement for operators to demonstrate sufficient breakup of the vehicle acts as an added layer of protection against multiple casualty events. Typically, deorbit produces extreme aerothermal and inertial forces that cause extensive breakup of vehicles that were not designed to survive substantially intact. However, extensive break-up is not always a guaranteed outcome. Therefore, an operator would be required to demonstrate that each piece of resulting debris from a UAR has a small enough effective casualty area to make multiple casualties an unlikely outcome. This demonstration would use the information already required by the debris analysis in accordance with § 450.121 and consequence analysis in § 450.135(b), so no additional analysis or application requirements would be needed. V. Regulatory Notices and Analyses A. Regulatory Impact Analysis E.O. 12866 (“Regulatory Planning and Review”) and E.O. 13563 (“Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review”) require agencies to regulate in the “most cost-effective manner,” to make a “reasoned determination that the benefits of the intended regulation justify its costs,” and to develop regulations that “impose the least burden on society.” The Office of Management and Budget has determined this proposed rule is not a significant regulatory action as defined in Section 3(f) of E.O. 12866. FAA is seeking comments on the following analysis. Currently, most applicants meet the requirement in § 450.101(c) to protect against high consequence events by ensuring that the consequence of any reasonably foreseeable failure mode, in any significant period of flight, is no greater than 1 x 10 −3 CE C . The proposed rule would allow an applicant to forgo this demonstration for a UAR if the applicant shows that there is sufficient breakup of the launch or reentry vehicle, including all vehicle components and undeployed payloads. The applicant would make the showing using the information already required by the debris analysis in accordance with § 450.121 and consequence analysis in § 450.135(b). Consequently, no additional analysis or application requirements would be needed. FAA estimates that forgoing the CE C demonstration for a UAR would save each applicant around 60 hours of labor. An aerospace engineer would complete this work. The base 2024 wage rate of a private industry worker working full-time as an aerospace engineer is $67.88 per hour. 2 When including benefits, the total compensation for an aerospace engineer 3 is $96.28 per hour. Therefore, the total cost savings for industry would be $5,777 per application. 2 “Employer Costs for Employee Compensation—May 2024,” Bureau of Labor Statistics, Employee costs for private industry workers in Series: 17-2011 Aerospace Engineers, available at: data.bls.gov/oes/#/industry/000000. 3 The total compensation includes Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) compensation data. For 2024, BLS estimates that wages make up 70.5 percent of total compensation while benefits make up 29.5 percent. Employer Costs for Employee Compensation—December 2024, available at: www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/ecec_03142025.htm. To calculate total compensation, FAA multiplies the base wage by a factor of 1.42 (rounded from 100/70.5). Therefore, the total compensation for an aerospace engineers is 96.28 per hour ($67.88 per hour × 1.42). For FAA, an aerospace engineer would take about 30 hours to provide guidance and review the data. The aerospace engineer is on the FAA Core Compensation Plan at a J band 4 with a base hourly rate of $95.33. FAA uses a factor of 1.3625 for benefits 5 which results in a total loaded hourly wage of $129.88. This results in total cost savings of $3,897 per application for FAA. Therefore, the total cost savings between FAA and an applicant would be $9,674 per application. Any cost savings would only impact new applicants, and FAA expects about 40 new applications in the next 5 years. However, not all applicants would apply to conduct operations where UARs are possible. Therefore, the total number of applications impacted would be less than 40. 4 FAA Engineering Pay Band J with Washington DC locality; effective Jan. 2026, maximum salary $198,281, available at: www.faa.gov/jobs/working_here/benefits/pay/core_salary_with_conversion.xlsx. 5 Update to Civilian Position Full Fringe Benefit Cost Factor, Federal Pay Raise Assumptions, and Inflation Factors used in OMB Circular No. A-76, “Performance of Commercial Activities”, Office of Management and Budget, March 11, 2008, available at: www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/legacy_drupal_files/omb/memoranda/2008/m08-13.pdf. B. Regulatory Flexibility Act Under the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) (5 U.S.C. 601-612), agencies must prepare and make available for public comment a regulatory flexibility analysis that describes the effect of the rulemaking on small entities ( i.e., small businesses, small organizations, and small government jurisdictions). No regulatory flexibility analysis is required, however, if the head of an agency certifies that the proposed rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. FAA has concluded and hereby certifies that this proposed rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities; therefore, an analysis is not included. C. International Trade Impact Assessment The Trade Agreements Act of 1979 (Pub. L. 96-39), as amended by the Uruguay Round Agreements Act (Pub. L. 103-465), prohibits Federal agencies from establishing standards or engaging in related activities that create unnecessary obstacles to the foreign commerce of the United States. Pursuant to these Acts, the establishment of standards is not considered an unnecessary obstacle to the foreign commerce of the United States, so long as the standard has a legitimate domestic objective, such as the protection of safety, and does not operate in a manner that excludes imports that meet this objective. The statute also requires consideration of international standards and, where appropriate, they be the basis for U.S. standards. FAA has assessed the potential effect of this proposed rule and determined that it would not create unnecessary obstacles to the foreign commerce of the United States. D. Unfunded Mandates Assessment The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (2 U.S.C. 1531-1538) governs the issuance of Federal regulations that require unfunded mandates. An unfunded mandate is a regulation that requires a State, local, or Tribal government or the private sector to incur direct costs without the Federal Government having first provided the funds to pay those costs. FAA determined the proposed rule would not result in the expenditure of $193,000,000 or more ($100,000,000 adjusted for inflation using the most current Implicit Price Deflator for the Gross Domestic Product) by State, local, or Tribal governments, in the aggregate, or the private sector, in any one year. E. Paperwork Reduction Act The Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (44 U.S.C. 3507(d)) requires FAA consider the impact of paperwork and other information collection burdens imposed on the public. FAA has determined there would be no new requirement for information collection associated with this proposed rule. F. International Compatibility In keeping with U.S. obligations under the Convention on International Civil Aviation, it is FAA policy to conform to International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Standards and Recommended Practices to the maximum extent practicable. FAA has determined there are no ICAO Standards and Recommended Practices that correspond to these proposed regulations. G. Environmental Analysis The Department has analyzed the environmental impacts of this notice of proposed rulemaking pursuant to the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA) (42 U.S.C. 4321, et seq. ). FAA has determined this proposed rule is categorically excluded pursuant to FAA Order 1050.1G. Categorical exclusions are categories of actions FAA has determined normally do not significantly affect the quality of the human environment and therefore do not require either an environmental assessment (EA) or environmental impact statement (EIS). In analyzing the applicability of a categorical exclusion, FAA must also consider whether extraordinary circumstances are present that would warrant the preparation of an EA or EIS. This rulemaking, which would allow a launch and reentry vehicle operator to protect against high consequence events during an uncontrolled atmospheric return by showing that there would be sufficient breakup of the vehicle to ensure protection against a single event expected to produce multiple casualties, is categorically excluded pursuant to FAA Order 1050.1G, Appendix B, Paragraph B-2.6(f), which categorically excludes issuance of regulatory documents. FAA does not anticipate any environmental impacts, and there are no extraordinary circumstances present in connection with this rulemaking. VI. E.O. Determinations A. E.O. 13132, Federalism FAA has analyzed this proposed rule under the principles and criteria of E.O. 13132, Federalism. FAA has determined this action would not have a substantial direct effect on the States, or the relationship between the Federal Government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government, and, therefore, would not have federalism implications. B. E.O. 13175, Consultation and Coordination With Indian Tribal Governments Consistent with E.O. 13175, Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments, 6 and FAA Order 1210.20, American Indian and Alaska Native Tribal Consultation Policy and Procedures, 7 FAA ensures Federally Recognized Tribes (Tribes) are given the opportunity to provide meaningful and timely input regarding proposed Federal actions that have the potential to affect uniquely or significantly their respective Tribes. At this point, FAA has not identified any unique or significant effects, environmental or otherwise, on Tribes resulting from this proposed rule. 6 65 FR 67249 (November 6, 2000). 7 FAA Order No. 1210.20 (January 28, 2004), available at: www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/1210.pdf. C. E.O. 13211, Regulations That Significantly Affect Energy Supply, Distribution, or Use FAA analyzed this proposed rule under E.O. 13211, Actions Concerning Regulations that Significantly Affect Energy Supply, Distribution, or Use (May 18, 2001). FAA has determined it would not be a “significant energy action” under the E.O. and would not be likely to have a significant adverse effect on the supply, distribution, or use of energy. D. E.O. 13609, Promoting International Regulatory Cooperation E.O. 13609, Promoting International Regulatory Cooperation, promotes international regulatory cooperation to (1) meet shared challenges involving health, safety, labor, security, environmental, and other issues and to reduce, eliminate, or (2) prevent unnecessary differences in regulatory requirements. FAA has analyzed this action under the policies and agency responsibilities of E.O. 13609 and has determined this action would have no effect on international regulatory cooperation. E. E.O. 14192, Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation This proposed rule, if finalized as proposed, is expected to be an E.O. 14192 deregulatory action because it has total costs less than zero as it streamlines the licensing process and reduces regulatory burden for license applicants. PART 450—LAUNCH AND REENTRY LICENSE REQUIREMENTS 3. The authority citation for part 450 is revised to read as follows: Authority: 51 U.S.C. Chapter 509. 4. Amend § 450.101 by revising paragraph (c) to read as follows: § 450.101 Safety criteria. (c) High consequence event protection. content: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION Federal Aviation Administration 14 CFR Part 450 [Docket No.: FAA-2026- 9937; Notice No. 26-24] RIN 2120-AM43 Flight Safety Limits Objectives Burden Reducing Clarification AGENCY: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT). ACTION: Notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM). SUMMARY: FAA proposes to amend its commercial space launch and reentry licensing regulations to streamline the licensing process and reduce regulatory burden for license applicants. Specifically, FAA proposes to clarify the requirements for establishing flight safety limits that define when a vehicle operator must initiate flight abort. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: I. Overview In accordance with Executive Order (E.O.) 14335, “Enabling Competition in the Commercial Space Industry,” FAA proposes to amend its commercial space launch and reentry regulations at 14 CFR part 450 to further streamline the commercial licensing process. The regulations at 14 CFR 450.108(c) require a vehicle operator to determine flight safety limits that define when the operator must initiate flight abort. To address applicant confusion about the meaning of 14 CFR 450.108(c)(4), FAA proposes to reword the paragraph to clarify which inputs are necessary for establishing flight safety limits to prevent high consequence events. II. Authority for This Rulemaking The Commercial Space Launch Act of 1984, as amended and codified at 51 U.S.C. 50901-50924, authorizes the Secretary of Transportation to oversee, license, and regulate commercial launch and reentry activities, and the operation of launch and reentry sites within the United States or as carried out by U.S. citizens. Section 50905 directs the Secretary to exercise this responsibility consistent with public health and safety, safety of property, and the national security and foreign policy interests of the United States. In addition, section 50903 requires the Secretary to encourage, facilitate, and promote commercial space launches and reentries by the private sector. As codified in 49 CFR 1.83(b), the Secretary has delegated authority to the FAA Administrator to carry out these functions. III. Background FAA has established commercial space regulations governing licensing of launch and reentry in 14 CFR chapter III. On December 10, 2020, FAA issued a final rule consolidating all substantive launch and reentry licensing regulations into a new part 450 (85 FR 79566) that went into effect on March 10, 2021. On August 13, 2025, the President issued E.O. 14335, “Enabling Competition in the Commercial Space Industry,” requiring the Secretary of Transportation to “reevaluate, amend, or rescind” the part 450 regulations for the purpose of further streamlining the commercial licensing process. This proposed rule is being published in furtherance of this E.O. Section 450.101(c) provides that an operator may use flight abort as a hazard control strategy to protect against a high consequence event in uncontrolled areas. 1 Flight abort accomplishes a controlled ending to vehicle flight, such as through explosive destruct. Section 450.108 provides requirements for flight abort, including requirements for flight safety limits. Flight safety limits, in this context, define the criteria under which a vehicle operator must initiate flight abort. 1 As defined by 14 CFR 401.7, an “uncontrolled area” is “an area of land not controlled by a launch or reentry operator, a launch or reentry site operator, an adjacent site operator, or other entity by agreement.” One of the requirements for flight abort, located at § 450.108(c)(4), provides that an operator must determine and use flight safety limits defining when the operator must initiate flight abort “to prevent conditional expected casualties (CE C ) greater than 1 × 10 −2 in uncontrolled areas due to flight abort or due to flight outside the limits of a useful mission from any reasonably foreseeable off-trajectory failure mode in any significant period of flight . . . .” The purpose of § 450.108(c)(4) is to ensure that, when an operator cannot develop flight safety limits that prevent hazards from affecting uncontrolled areas, the flight safety limits nonetheless protect against high consequence events in uncontrolled areas. The paragraph asks operators to compute the CE C in each significant period of flight 2 where flight abort or flight outside the limits of a useful mission 3 may be an outcome for each reasonably foreseeable off-trajectory failure mode. 4 If the maximum CE C developed through this method is not greater than 1 × 10 −2 , an operator can demonstrate high consequence event protection. If this analysis does not demonstrate compliance with high consequence event protection, an operator may modify the limits of a useful mission or flight safety limits, and an operator should update the flight safety limits analysis accordingly until compliance with § 450.108(c)(4) can be demonstrated. 2 As discussed in the final rule establishing part 450 “Streamlined Launch and Reentry Requirements” (85 FR 79566), a period of flight is considered significant if it is long enough for a mitigation, such as flight abort, to decrease the public risks or consequences materially from any reasonably foreseeable failure mode (85 FR 79566, 79604). 3 As defined by 14 CFR 401.7, a “useful mission” means “a mission that can attain one or more objectives.” The “limits of a useful mission,” as defined by that section, means “the trajectory data or other parameters that bound the performance of a useful mission, including flight azimuth limits.” The limits of a useful mission are developed as part of the flight safety analysis under 14 CFR 450.119. 4 As discussed in the final rule establishing part 450 “Streamlined Launch and Reentry Requirements” (85 FR 79566), an off-trajectory failure is a failure “for which a vehicle deviates from its intended flight path—for example, due to failures of the guidance, navigation, or control systems” (85 FR 79566, 79620). Failure modes are categories of hazardous events that share significant similarity in cause and system response, prior to consideration of mitigations or hazard control strategies. Therefore an “off-trajectory failure mode” is a failure mode where a vehicle deviates from its intended flight path. AC 450.101-1, High Consequence Event Protection, provides additional background on “failure modes” and how applicants may identify “reasonably foreseeable” failure modes. However, the phrasing of paragraph (c)(4) has led some applicants to misinterpret the paragraph as requiring two separate CE C calculations: one for outcomes resulting in flight abort and one for outcomes that result in flight outside the limits of a useful mission. Meanwhile, other applicants have interpreted the paragraph to mean that an applicant may select only one of these two outcomes and ignore the other in CE C calculations. In AC 450.108-1, Flight Abort Rule Development, FAA attempted to clarify the requirement, writing that “[t]he CE C results from various end states, such as break-up due to aerodynamic loads or FSS activation, from flight abort and flight outside the limits of a useful mission should be averaged together to compute the mean CE C for each significant period of flight.” However, misinterpretations of the rule have persisted and led to repeated exchanges with the applicants, requiring additional time and effort to develop an acceptable application. IV. Discussion of the Proposal The proposed rule would reword § 450.108(c)(4) to reduce confusion among applicants regarding how to comply with the requirement. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: I. Overview In accordance with Executive Order (E.O.) 14335 “Enabling Competition in the Commercial Space Industry,” FAA proposes to amend its commercial space launch and reentry regulations at 14 CFR part 450 to further streamline the commercial licensing process. Currently, 14 CFR 450.108(e) provides that a vehicle operator using flight abort as a hazard control strategy is not required to initiate flight abort to protect against high consequence events once certain conditions are met. The proposed rule would clarify that the exception in paragraph (e) applies only to a phase of flight in which the conditions are present. II. Authority for This Rulemaking The Commercial Space Launch Act of 1984, as amended and codified at 51 U.S.C. 50901-50924, authorizes the Secretary of Transportation to oversee, license, and regulate commercial launch and reentry activities, and the operation of launch and reentry sites within the United States (U.S.) or as carried out by U.S. citizens. Section 50905 directs the Secretary to exercise this responsibility consistent with public health and safety, safety of property, and the national security and foreign policy interests of the United States. In addition, section 50903 requires the Secretary to encourage, facilitate, and promote commercial space launches and reentries by the private sector. As codified in 49 CFR 1.83(b), the Secretary has delegated authority to the FAA Administrator to carry out these functions. III. Background FAA has established commercial space regulations governing licensing of launch and reentry in 14 CFR chapter III. On December 10, 2020, FAA issued a final rule consolidating all substantive launch and reentry licensing regulations into a new part 450 (85 FR 79566) that went into effect on March 10, 2021. On August 13, 2025, the President issued E.O. 14335, “Enabling Competition in the Commercial Space Industry,” requiring the Secretary of Transportation to “reevaluate, amend, or rescind” the part 450 regulations for the purpose of further streamlining the commercial licensing process. This proposed rule is being published in furtherance of this E.O. Section 450.101(c) provides that an operator may use flight abort as a hazard control strategy to protect against a high consequence event in uncontrolled areas. Flight abort accomplishes a controlled ending to vehicle flight, such as through explosive destruct. Section 450.108 provides requirements for flight abort, including requirements for flight safety limits. Flight safety limits, in this context, define the criteria under which a vehicle operator must initiate flight abort. For some mission scenarios, at some point in flight, flight abort can no longer mitigate risk, and applicants may wish to turn off the flight abort system to prevent accidental initiation of the abort system. This possibility is addressed by § 450.108(e), which states that a flight does not need to be aborted to protect against high consequence events beginning immediately after critical vehicle parameters are validated, if the vehicle is able to achieve a useful mission, and if, for the remainder of flight: (1) flight abort would not materially decrease the risk from a high consequence event; and (2) there are no key flight safety events. To meet the first condition that flight abort would not materially decrease the risk of a high consequence event for the remainder of flight, an operator should perform a comparison of the risk ( i.e., expected casualties (E C )) with and without flight abort from failure modes that produce conditional expected casualties (CE C ) greater than 0.01. If flight abort would not reduce E C associated with each failure mode materially, then this condition is met. To meet the second condition, an operator must demonstrate that the remainder of flight does not include any “key flight safety event,” which is defined in 14 CFR 401.7 to mean “a flight activity that has an increased likelihood of causing a failure compared with other portions of flight.” However, even if these conditions are satisfied for the remainder of flight, an operator is only permitted to switch off the flight abort system if, during flight, the operator is able to validate “critical vehicle parameters,” meaning parameters that demonstrate the vehicle is capable of completing safe flight through the upcoming phase of flight where population is exposed to hazardous debris effects from reasonably foreseeable failure modes. IV. Discussion of the Proposal The proposed rule maintains the essential requirements and structure of § 450.108(e), with two minor revisions. First, the proposed rule would change the title of § 450.108(e) from “End of flight abort” to “End of flight safety limits” to match the intention of the paragraph more closely. Paragraph (e) does not require an operator to turn off flight abort capability or eliminate flight abort as a hazard control strategy, as unintentionally suggested by the current title, but rather describes conditions under which an operator is not required to set flight safety limits to protect against high consequence events in uncontrolled areas during some subsequent phases of flight. Second, the proposed rule would also scope paragraph (e) to apply only to a phase of flight rather than “the remainder of flight,” as the paragraph currently states. Current paragraph (e) was drafted with the understanding that most operators would only turn off the flight abort capability at the end of a flight, such as the phase immediately before orbital insertion. However, FAA anticipates that operators may seek to turn off flight abort capability during one phase of flight and turn it back on during a subsequent phase. As such, this revision would provide additional flexibility to operators while preserving public safety by explicitly accommodating this practice. This proposal, therefore, would amend paragraph (e) to say that a flight does not need to be aborted for the remainder of a phase of flight if the specified conditions are present during that phase. title: Technical Corrections of Commercial Space Transportation Regulations
content: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION Federal Aviation Administration 14 CFR Parts 413, 414, 450, and 460 [Docket No.: FAA-2026-7035; Amdt. Nos. 413-15, 414-5, 450-4, 460-5] RIN 2120-AM32 Technical Corrections of Commercial Space Transportation Regulations AGENCY: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Department of Transportation (DOT). ACTION: Final rule; technical amendment. SUMMARY: This final rule contains technical corrections in FAA regulations. DATES: Effective November 9, 2026. ADDRESSES: For further information on where to obtain copies of rulemaking document and other information related to this final rule, see “Additional Information” in the SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION section of this document. FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Lisa Cacciatore, Office of Commercial Space Transportation, Federal Aviation Administration, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590; telephone (202) 880-1489; email Lisa.E.Cacciatore@faa.gov. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: I. Executive Summary A. Overview of the Final Rule FAA is amending the authority citations in parts 413, 414, and 450 to include 51 U.S.C. 50924. In addition, FAA has identified six technical corrections to parts 413, 414, 450, and 460. These technical corrections are non-substantive in nature and are intended to correct typographical errors, clarify regulatory text, and ensure consistency. The changes correct mistakes and omissions and clarify the regulations published in the part 450 final rule. 1 1 Streamlined Launch and Reentry License Requirements, 85 FR 79566 (December 10, 2020) (hereby referred to as “SLR2”). B. Summary of the Costs and Benefits This final rule makes non-substantive technical corrections to correct typographical errors, clarify regulatory text, and ensure consistency. FAA expects no additional costs for the public or FAA because these changes do not affect existing regulatory requirements. II. Authority for This Rulemaking and 5 U.S.C. 553 Implementation Exceptions A. Authority for This Rulemaking The Commercial Space Launch Act of 1984, as amended and codified at 51 U.S.C. 50901-50924 (the Act), authorizes the Secretary of Transportation (Secretary) to oversee, license, and regulate commercial launch and reentry activities, and the operation of launch and reentry sites within the United States (U.S.) or as carried out by U.S. citizens. Section 50905 directs the Secretary to exercise this responsibility consistent with public health and safety, safety of property, and the national security and foreign policy interests of the United States. In addition, section 50903 requires the Secretary to encourage, facilitate, and promote commercial space launches and reentries by the private sector. As codified in 49 CFR 1.83(b), the Secretary has delegated authority to the FAA Administrator to carry out these functions. B. Good Cause Exemption per 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B) Section 553(b)(B) of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) (5 U.S.C.) authorizes agencies to dispense with notice and comment procedures for rulemakings when the agency for “good cause” finds those procedures to be “impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.” Under this section, an agency, upon finding good cause, may issue a final rule without seeking comment prior to the rulemaking. FAA has concluded that notice and comment is unnecessary for this rulemaking. Courts have consistently recognized that notice and comment are unnecessary where a rule makes only technical, clerical, or nonsubstantive changes that do not alter the rights or obligations of regulated entities and are unlikely to generate meaningful public input. 2 For example, in Utility Solid Waste Activities Group v. EPA, the D.C. Circuit explained that the “unnecessary” prong applies where the regulated community has “little or nothing to say” regarding the agency's action because the rule does not implicate substantive policy choices. 3 In Mack Trucks, Inc v. EPA, the D.C. Circuit cautioned that the unnecessary exception must be narrowly construed, but made clear that its application is appropriate where notice and comment would serve no practical purpose. 4 2 Utility Solid Waste Activities Group v. EPA, 236 F.3d 749, 754 (D.C. Cir. 2001); Mack Trucks, Inc. v. EPA, 682 F. 3d 87, 93 (D.C. Cir. 2012). 3 236 F.3d 749, 754 (D.C. Cir. 2001). 4 Courts have held that the unnecessary prong of good cause must be “confined to those situations in which the administrative rule is a routine determination, insignificant in nature and impact, and inconsequential to the industry and to the public.” Mack Trucks, Inc. v. EPA, 682 F.3d 87, 94 (D.C. Cir. 2012) (quoting Util. Solid Waste Activities Grp., 236 F.3d at 755). The technical amendments in this final rule correct incorrect words, remove unnecessary references, and clarify the purpose of the text to conform to the statutory requirements. These amendments do not reflect a change in policy judgment, nor do they affect how regulated parties comply with FAA requirements. Thus, FAA has determined that this rule is suitable for a final rulemaking because these changes are noncontroversial and a notice and comment period is unnecessary. C. Effective Upon Publication per 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3) The APA generally requires that a substantive rule be published at least 30 days before its effective date. However, 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3) permits an agency to make a rule effective less than 30 days after publication for good cause. As discussed in the previous section, FAA has found good cause for forgoing notice and comment under 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B). For these same reasons, FAA finds good cause under 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3) to make this rule effective immediately upon publication in the Federal Register . III. Background A. History In 2018, Space Policy Directive-2 (SPD-2) directed FAA to streamline and modernize commercial space launch and reentry licensing. As a result, in 2020, FAA published Streamlined Launch and Reentry License Requirements, 85 FR 79566 (the SLR2 final rule). The SLR2 final rule, codified as part 450, streamlined and increased flexibility in FAA commercial space launch and reentry regulations and removed obsolete requirements. It consolidated and revised multiple regulatory parts and applied a single set of licensing and safety regulations across several types of operations and vehicles. Part 450 provides the requirements to obtain a vehicle operator license, the safety requirements, and the terms and conditions of a vehicle operator license. On August 13, 2025, the President issued Executive Order (E.O.) 14335, “Enabling Competition in the Commercial Space Industry,” which requires the Secretary of Transportation to “reevaluate, amend, or rescind” the regulations in part 450 for the purpose of further streamlining the commercial licensing process. As part of FAA's response to this directive, FAA is making non-substantive, technical revisions to its regulations to correct errors and improve clarity. These changes do not modify existing compliance obligations or impose new requirements; rather, they are intended to ensure that FAA regulations remain accurate, clear, and effective. IV. Discussion of the Final Rule A. Correction to Part 413, License Application Procedures FAA is amending 14 CFR 413.7(d)(1) through (3) by replacing the term “safety approval” with “safety element approval” in each instance that it occurs. In the SLR2 final rule, FAA replaced the term “safety approval” with “safety element approval” in a number of instances to distinguish between two types of approvals falling under the term “safety approval.” Prior to the SLR2 final rule, “safety approval” could refer to either (1) an FAA determination that an applicant is capable of launching a launch or reentry vehicle and its payload without jeopardizing public health and safety and safety of property or (2) the approval of a “safety element,” as that term is defined in § 414.3. The SLR2 final rule differentiated these usages by using the term “safety approval” to capture the former meaning, and “safety element approval” to capture the latter meaning. However, the SLR2 final rule inadvertently omitted this terminology change in § 413.7(d), which discusses how an applicant may incorporate a safety element approval into a license application. This rule corrects that omission by replacing the term “safety approval” in § 413.7(d) with “safety element approval” in each instance that it occurs. The correction does not represent a substantive change in the rule because the other language in § 413.7(d) clearly indicates that the paragraph only relates to safety element approvals. B. Correction to § 414.43(c), Submissions; Oral Presentations in Safety Element Approval Applications The procedures by which applicants may obtain a safety element approval and renew and transfer an existing safety element approval are set forth in 14 CFR part 414. Subpart D of part 414 describes the procedures for appealing a decision by FAA regarding safety element approval. Section 414.41(a) states that FAA will give a safety element approval applicant or holder notice of its decision to deny, modify, suspend, or revoke a safety element approval. Section 414.41(b) states that the applicant or holder is entitled to a determination on the record after opportunity for a hearing. Section 414.43 describes the process by which the determination on the record will be handled, including paragraph (c) of that section, which states that “[p]etitions [for a determination by an administrative law judge] must be filed as soon as practicable, but in no event more than 30 days after issuance of decision or finding under § 414.37.” FAA is replacing the reference to § 414.37 in § 414.43(c) with a reference to § 414.41. In the SLR2 final rule, FAA renumbered part 414, including renumbering previous § 414.37 as current § 414.41. However, the cross-reference to § 414.37 in § 414.43(c) was inadvertently not updated to match the renumbering. The change is nonsubstantive because FAA has consistently maintained that retention of the cross-reference to § 414.37 was unintentional and the result of a drafting oversight in the SLR2 rulemaking. C. Correction to § 450.101, Safety Criteria Section 450.101 provides the safety criteria for launch and reentry vehicles, with launch vehicles addressed in § 450.101(a) and reentry vehicles in § 450.101(b). When the SLR2 final rule was published, it inadvertently included a reference to “launch vehicle” in § 450.101(b)(2). Given that § 450.101(b) addresses risk criteria for reentry vehicles, it is incorrect for this section to reference the proposed flight of a launch vehicle. This rule changes the phrase “flight of a launch vehicle” to “deorbit of a reentry vehicle” in § 450.101(b)(2). FAA intended for “reentry vehicle” to be used in § 450.101(b)(2) but inadvertently used the term “launch vehicle” instead. Since the adoption of § 450.101(b)(2), FAA has applied the regulation to reentry vehicles as originally intended. This correction will formally remedy the error and reduce the risk of confusion. D. Correction to § 450.173(f), Mishap Plan—Reporting, Response, and Investigation Requirements Section 450.173(f) outlines the requirements for an applicant's mishap plan, including reporting, response, and investigation requirements. When the SLR2 final rule was published, FAA used the word “preventative” in the title of § 450.173(f), but the word “preventive” in the text of § 450.173(f). While both words can be used interchangeably, FAA wants to ensure consistency and clarity in its regulations. This change provides consistent usage by changing the word “preventive” in the text of § 450.173(f) to “preventative,” so that it matches the title of the subsection. E. Correction to § 450.207, Human Space Flight Requirements Section 450.207 requires an applicant be in compliance with part 460 for licensees conducting launches or reentries with humans on board. The regulation is currently written with “spaceflight” as one word both in the title and in the text of § 450.207. However, “space flight” is two words throughout the rest of part 450. In order to be consistent throughout part 450, this rule changes “spaceflight” to “space flight” in both the title and text of § 450.207. F. Corrections to Part 460, Human Space Flight Requirements Section 460.45 requires that an operator inform each space flight participant in writing about the risks of the launch and reentry, including the safety record of the launch or reentry vehicle type. In the SLR2 final rule, FAA adopted a new definition of “mishap” for the purposes of part 450. As part of this, FAA incorporated the prior definitions of accident and incident into the new “mishap” definition. In addition, FAA updated the broader part 400 regulations to remove the terms “accident” and “incident” from regulations that applied to part 450 operations, because those terms were no longer defined. However, FAA inadvertently failed to update § 460.45(e) in the SLR2 final rule. This rule corrects § 460.45(e) by replacing the phrase “accidents and human space flight incidents” with the phrase “events that meet any of paragraph (1), (4), (5), or (8) of the definition of `mishap' in § 401.7 of this chapter.” This amendment aligns the language of § 460.45(e) with the defined terms applicable to part 450. G. Amendments to Authority Citations Lastly, FAA is revising the authority citations for parts 413, 414, 450, and 460 from “51 U.S.C. 50901-50923” to 51 U.S.C. 509.” The Commercial Space Launch Act of 1984 (“CSLA”), Public Law 98-575, authorizes the Secretary of Transportation to oversee, license, and regulate commercial launch and reentry activities, and the operation of launch and reentry sites. In 1994, the CSLA was codified at 49 U.S.C. ch. 701 ( see Pub. L. 103-272), which was subsequently transferred to 51 U.S.C. 509 in 2010 ( see Pub. L. 111-314). At that time, Chapter 509 contained sections 50901 through 50923. In 2025, a new section 50924 was added to Chapter 509 by Public Law 119-21, commonly known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. FAA is amending the authority citations to account for this new section. However, rather than updating the authority citations to state the number of this new section ( i.e., 51 U.S.C. 50901-50924), FAA has determined that the authority citations should instead point to 51 U.S.C. 509. This change will prevent FAA from needing to update the authority citations each time a new section is added to 51 U.S.C. 509. V. Regulatory Notices and Analyses A. Regulatory Impact Analysis E.O. 12866 (“Regulatory Planning and Review”) and E.O. 13563 (“Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review”) require agencies to regulate in the “most cost-effective manner,” to make a “reasoned determination that the benefits of the intended regulation justify its costs,” and to develop regulations that “impose the least burden on society.” The Office of Management and Budget has determined that this rule is not a significant regulatory action as defined in section (3)(f) of E.O. 12866. This final rule is considered an E.O. 14192 deregulatory action. Table 1 lists the changes to each provision along with their respective impacts. Because these are technical corrections addressing typographical errors, clarifying regulatory text, and ensuring consistency, there are no additional costs to industry and FAA. Table 1—Regulatory Changes and Impact Provision Change Impact 14 CFR 413.7(d)—Correct Safety Element Approval name Amends § 413.7(d)(1) through (d)(3), by adding the word “element” to the phrase “safety approval” No impact. 14 CFR 414.43—Correction to reference Amends the reference to § 414.37 in § 414.43(c) by changing it to § 414.41 No impact. 14 CFR 450.101—Correct error in Reentry Risk Criteria Amends § 450.101(b)(2) by changing the phrase “flight of a launch vehicle” to “deorbit of a reentry vehicle” Small administrative cost savings because it provides clarity to regulated entities. FAA will not have to provide guidance to clarify any confusion from regulated entities. 14 CFR 450.173(f)—Correct terminology in Mishap Plan Corrects § 450.173(f) by changing the word “preventive” in the sentence to “preventative” No impact. 14 CFR 450.207—Correct terminology for consistency in Human Space Flight Regulations Corrects § 450.207 by changing the word “spaceflight” to the phrase “space flight” to be consistent with the rest of the final rule No impact. 14 CFR 460—Correct Mishap terminology in Human Space Flight Regulations Corrects § 460.45(e) by replacing the phrase “accidents and human space flight incidents” with the phrase “events that meet any of paragraph (1), (4), (5), or (8) of the definition of ‘mishap’ in § 401.7 of this chapter” No impact. B. Regulatory Flexibility Act The Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA), in 5 U.S.C. 603, requires an agency to prepare an initial regulatory flexibility analysis describing impacts on small entities whenever 5 U.S.C. 553 or any other law requires an agency to publish a general notice of proposed rulemaking for any proposed rule. Similarly, 5 U.S.C. 604 requires an agency to prepare a final regulatory flexibility analysis when an agency issues a final rule under 5 U.S.C. 553 after that section or any other law requires publication of a general notice of proposed rulemaking. FAA concludes good cause exists to forgo notice and comment and to not delay the effective date for this rule. As 5 U.S.C. 553 does not require notice and comment in this situation, 5 U.S.C. 603 and 604 similarly do not require regulatory flexibility analyses. C. International Trade Impact Assessment The Trade Agreements Act of 1979 (Pub. L. 96-39), as amended by the Uruguay Round Agreements Act (Pub. L. 103-465), prohibits Federal agencies from establishing standards or engaging in related activities that create unnecessary obstacles to the foreign commerce of the United States. Pursuant to these Acts, the establishment of standards is not considered an unnecessary obstacle to the foreign commerce of the United States, so long as the standard has a legitimate domestic objective, such as the protection of safety, and does not operate in a manner that excludes imports that meet this objective. The statute also requires consideration of international standards and, where appropriate, that they be the basis for U.S. standards. FAA has assessed the potential effect of this rule and determined it ensures the safety of the American public and does not exclude imports that meet this objective. As a result, FAA does not consider this rule as creating an unnecessary obstacle to foreign commerce. D. Unfunded Mandates Assessment The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (2 U.S.C. 1531-1538) governs the issuance of Federal regulations that require unfunded mandates. An unfunded mandate is a regulation that requires a State, local, or Tribal government or the private sector to incur direct costs without the Federal Government having first provided the funds to pay those costs. FAA determined the rule will not result in the expenditure of $193,000,000 or more ($100,000,000 adjusted for inflation using the most current Implicit Price Deflator for the Gross Domestic Product) by State, local, or Tribal governments, in the aggregate, or the private sector, in any one year. E. Paperwork Reduction Act The Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (44 U.S.C. 3507(d)) requires FAA consider the impact of paperwork and other information collection burdens imposed on the public. FAA has determined there is no new requirement for information collection associated with this final rule. F. International Compatibility In keeping with U.S. obligations under the Convention on International Civil Aviation, it is FAA policy to conform to International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Standards and Recommended Practices to the maximum extent practicable. FAA has determined there are no ICAO Standards and Recommended Practices that correspond to these regulations. G. Environmental Analysis The Department has analyzed the environmental impacts of this final rule pursuant to the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA) (42 U.S.C. 4321 et seq. ). FAA has determined this rule is categorically excluded pursuant to FAA Order 1050.1G. Categorical exclusions are categories of actions FAA has determined normally do not significantly affect the quality of the human environment and therefore do not require either an environmental assessment (EA) or environmental impact statement (EIS).1 In analyzing the applicability of a categorical exclusion, FAA must also consider whether extraordinary circumstances are present that would warrant the preparation of an EA or EIS.2 This rulemaking, which makes minor nonsubstantive technical edits to FAA's commercial space regulations, is categorically excluded pursuant to FAA Order 1050.1G, Appendix B, Paragraph B-2.6(f), which categorically excludes issuance of regulatory documents. FAA does not anticipate any environmental impacts, and there are no extraordinary circumstances present in connection with this rulemaking. VI. E.O. Determinations A. E.O. 13132, Federalism FAA has analyzed this final rule under the principles and criteria of E.O. 13132, Federalism. FAA has determined this action will not have a substantial direct effect on the States, or the relationship between the Federal Government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government, and, therefore, will not have federalism implications. B. E.O. 13175, Consultation and Coordination With Indian Tribal Governments Consistent with E.O. 13175, Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments, 5 and FAA Order 1210.20, American Indian and Alaska Native Tribal Consultation Policy and Procedures, 6 FAA ensures that Federally Recognized Tribes (Tribes) are given the opportunity to provide meaningful and timely input regarding proposed Federal actions that have the potential to have substantial direct effects on one or more Tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Tribes; or to affect uniquely or significantly their respective Tribes. At this point, FAA has not identified any unique or significant effects, environmental or otherwise, on Tribes resulting from this final rule. 5 65 FR 67249 (Nov. 6, 2000). 6 FAA Order No. 1210.20 (Jan. 28, 2004), available at www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/1210.pdf. C. E.O. 13211, Regulations That Significantly Affect Energy Supply, Distribution, or Use FAA analyzed this final rule under E.O. 13211, Actions Concerning Regulations that Significantly Affect Energy Supply, Distribution, or Use (May 18, 2001). FAA has determined it is not a “significant energy action” under the E.O. and is not likely to have a significant adverse effect on the supply, distribution, or use of energy. D. E.O. 13609, Promoting International Regulatory Cooperation Executive Order 13609, Promoting International Regulatory Cooperation, promotes international regulatory cooperation to meet shared challenges involving health, safety, labor, security, environmental, and other issues and to reduce, eliminate, or prevent unnecessary differences in regulatory requirements. FAA has analyzed this action under the policies and agency responsibilities of E.O. 13609 and has determined this action will have no effect on international regulatory cooperation. VII.
